meta.title: THE SOUL SURVEY
meta.tagline: A topographic survey of the collective soul, conducted in objective data.
meta.manifesto: Every act leaves a coordinate. A birth, a search, a warehouse, a crash — each one lands somewhere, and the landing is recorded. Alone, each record is trivia. Stacked, they become relief: ridgelines of genius, basins of grief, the bright grid of the machines we serve and that serve us. This is not a map of the land. It is a map of what we do on it. Toggle the layers. Watch the country change shape. The terrain is us.

themes.name: Memory
themes.reading: where the remembered entered the world

themes.name: Desire
themes.reading: what each place wants more than everywhere else

themes.name: Power
themes.reading: where the machines and the money live

themes.name: Omen
themes.reading: what we named the land when we were afraid

themes.name: Wonder
themes.reading: what we see when we look up

readings.title: Orientation
readings.text: {n} instruments, one terrain. Each layer is a real dataset with coordinates. Density becomes elevation; overlap becomes light. Watch them arrive.

readings.title: The Corridor of Grief
readings.text: The fulfillment network follows the interstates — and so does death. The same asphalt carries the packages and collects the toll. Orange and red are the same roads seen twice: once as commerce, once as grief.

readings.title: The Capital of the Internet
readings.text: One stretch of Northern Virginia answers most of the questions you ask the internet. Power is cheap, land is flat, fiber is thick — and the cloud condenses along the Potomac. The new AI campuses are landing in the same basin, like sediment.

readings.title: The Dark States
readings.text: In 2025 the most complete public record of American desire developed holes: Pornhub blocks access in 22 age-verification states, and its map went dark there. The hatched states are not empty of desire — they are empty of measurement. Censorship, rendered as cartography.

readings.title: Where Memory Pools
readings.text: Five thousand years of remembered births, and most of them pool in a triangle you could cross in a week. Paris alone holds 28,055. Memory is not a meritocracy of geography — it flows toward courts, ports, and printing presses.

readings.title: Devil's Country
readings.text: When surveyors named the arid West they reached for hell: 1,922 devils against 809 angels, and the devils cluster in the canyons and badlands where the land fought back. Fear got the dramatic terrain. Hope settled in the valleys.

readings.title: The Great Sorting
readings.text: Every year America quietly trades about a million households between its counties. The arcs are the trades; teal counties are inhaling, ember counties are exhaling. The Sun Belt breathes in; the old cores breathe out. Follow any single arc and it is a moving truck, a job taken, a goodbye said in a driveway.

readings.title: The Ledger of Betrayals
readings.text: So many ways to steal a town, every one on this map ending in a conviction. Dixon, Illinois is the archetype: $53.7 million siphoned over 22 years by the city comptroller, spent on champion quarter horses, in a town of sixteen thousand. The ledger names only the convicted, cites every line, and asks the only question that matters: who was supposed to be watching?

readings.title: The Arsenal and the Altar
readings.text: Two geographies of devotion, drawn from license rolls and pew counts. Steel points are the places that sell arms; the candle-gold wash is the density of the faithful. Sometimes they are the same places, sometimes opposites — the survey only shows where, and lets you argue about why.

readings.title: Who Knows Whom
readings.text: Economic connectedness asks one question of a county: do its poorer residents have friends who are not poor? At 1.0, friendship ignores class entirely. Only one county in six reaches it. The state averages run from 0.56 in South Carolina to 1.09 in New Hampshire, and the Upper Midwest and the mountain West glow while the Deep South stays pale. The map measures who knows whom, which is not the same as who helps whom.

layers.title: Where the Remembered Were Born
layers.caveat: visibility scoring favors the recently famous; 25.6% of source records lack coordinates

essay.what: The birthplaces of 1,704,189 notable humans — everyone with a verified Wikipedia/Wikidata footprint born between 3500 BC and 2018 AD, from the cross-verified database of notable people (Laouenan et al., Scientific Data, 2022). Every golden grain is a place that produced someone the world still remembers. The 12,000 most visible burn as distinct stars.
essay.how: 2,291,817 records streamed and aggregated to 0.25° cells; 74.4% carry verified birth coordinates. Brightness follows log density. Star selection uses the database's composite visibility score across five criteria — which favors the recently famous, and we disclose it: memory's spotlight is aimed at the present. Use the era scrubber to walk the nebula through five thousand years. A calling lens sorts the 5,000 brightest into nine groups folded from their Pantheon domains (screen, music, letters, art, thought and science, sport, power, faith, other); the fold is the survey's own and is listed in pipeline/build.py.
essay.why: Memory has a geography. It pools where rivers meet, where ports open, where empires kept their books — Paris alone holds 28,055 remembered births, more than most nations. Genius is not sown evenly; it is watered by cities. The nebula argues something uncomfortable: the world remembers people from places that were already powerful.

layers.title: The Last Speakers
layers.statline: {n} languages, every one a way of seeing
layers.caveat: one representative point per language, not a territory; endangerment as Glottolog's agglomerated status (AES)

essay.what: 7,836 languages, each placed where Glottolog puts its heart, coloured by how close it is to silence: from not endangered through threatened, shifting, moribund and nearly extinct to extinct. 983 are already gone. Another 2,520 are shifting, moribund or nearly extinct — spoken mostly by grandparents.
essay.how: Glottolog 5.3 (Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology), read as CLDF: every language-level languoid that is a spoken first language or a sign language, with Glottolog's coordinate and its Agglomerated Endangerment Status, which folds three expert catalogues (EGIDS, UNESCO, ElCat) into six steps. Pidgins, unattested and artificial languages are left out.
essay.why: Papua New Guinea alone holds 849 of these points, more than any other country. The red and grey sit where empires and settlers arrived: Australia has lost 227 languages, the United States 135, Brazil 95. Each grey point is a way of naming the world that no one alive can use. This is the survey's light side and its loss in one layer: the remembered, at the scale of a people.

layers.title: The Geography of Desire
layers.caveat: 22 states unmeasured — access blocked; countries show top relative categories

essay.what: The top disproportionate search term per state — what each place seeks more than the rest of the country does — from Pornhub Insights' 2025 Year in Review, plus the top relative category for the 20 most-visiting countries. Recorded verbatim. Text only.
essay.how: Read from the official year-in-review infographic (via archive; the live site refuses this container) and cross-checked against independent press republications, zero discrepancies. Countries carry relative categories because that is what Pornhub publishes at country level.
essay.why: Desire is regional — it borrows local accents, local nostalgia, local taboos. But the loudest data on this map is the silence: 22 states are dark because Pornhub blocks access where age-verification laws passed. Desire didn't vanish there. The measurement did. Legislation has redrawn the map of what can be known, and the gray states are a new terra incognita — the first layer of this survey to be censored in real time.

layers.title: Where the Cloud Touches Ground
layers.caveat: OpenStreetMap completeness follows mapping effort; centroids, not entrances

essay.what: 4,342 data centers with ground coordinates, worldwide: 4,244 mapped by OpenStreetMap contributors, plus 98 of the newest US hyperscale and AI campuses — xAI Colossus, Stargate sites — from the Brockovich accountability map, which tracks what OSM hasn't surveyed yet.
essay.how: Overpass API over telecom=data_center and building=data_center, nodes, ways and relations, deduplicated within 200 meters. Community-mapped data inherits community bias: coverage follows mapping effort, so Europe and North America are sharpest. © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL. The operator lens reads OpenStreetMap's own operator tag (2,634 of 4,342 facilities carry one) rather than guessing from names; joint ventures are filed under one named partner (the OpenAI campuses under Oracle) and shown in full on hover. A second lens isolates the 98 AI campuses from the Brockovich records: 33 operating, 65 under construction.
essay.why: The cloud is a place. It hums in Northern Virginia — Ashburn is the true capital of the internet — and clusters wherever power is cheap, land is flat, and fiber is thick. Every question you ask online is answered somewhere on this map. Notice the new AI campuses landing in the same basins: the machines settle like sediment, in layers, along the same rivers of electricity.

layers.title: The Thrones of Capital
layers.caveat: city-level coordinates; FY2024 revenue per Fortune methodology

essay.what: All 500 headquarters of the 2025 Fortune 500, each sized by revenue. Walmart sits at rank 1 with $680,985 million — a single company out-earning the GDP of most countries.
essay.how: Fortune's own 2025 ranking (fiscal-year 2024 revenue), 100% geocoded to city coordinates, 100% revenue coverage, zero companies dropped. Point area scales with revenue; the map is honest about hierarchy.
essay.why: Capital keeps addresses. Five hundred corporations, thirty-odd metros — the thrones sit clustered in a handful of skylines while their consequences spread everywhere else on this map: the warehouses they command, the data centers they rent, the towns they leave. Toggle Motion on top of this layer and watch command become circulation.

layers.title: The World's Furnaces
layers.statline: {n} power plants, sized by what they can burn
layers.caveat: frozen in 2021 (WRI no longer maintains the database); nameplate capacity, not generation; small plants unevenly covered outside the U.S. and Europe

essay.what: 34,936 power plants in 167 countries, each sized by the electricity it can make and coloured by what it burns or catches: coal, gas, oil, nuclear, hydro, wind, solar. Together they could deliver about 5.7 terawatts — the furnace under every other layer of this map.
essay.how: The World Resources Institute's Global Power Plant Database v1.3.0, built from national registries, the Global Energy Observatory, Enipedia and WRI's own work, under CC-BY 4.0. Fuels are folded into eight groups (petcoke with oil; biomass, waste, geothermal, storage and tidal under other). Names are kept for plants of 50 MW or more; capacity is nameplate, not generation. The database has been frozen since 2021: coal plants closed since and the solar and wind built since are missing.
essay.why: Lay the data centers on top: the cloud settles where the furnaces already burn. China holds 956 gigawatts of coal capacity — almost four times the United States — while the U.S. lists the most plants of any country, partly because its national registry reaches down to the smallest solar farms. The bright red knots are where the world's electricity is still made from fire.

layers.title: The Fulfillment Bloodstream
layers.caveat: facility types inferred from code shape; square footage unavailable

essay.what: 314 active Amazon US logistics facilities — 217 fulfillment centers, 70 sortation centers, 27 inbound cross-docks — the physical bloodstream of same-day desire.
essay.how: Verified facility codes from live FBA shipment routing (fba.wiki reference), geocoded 100% to city coordinates. The classic industry source, MWPVL, withdrew its public tables — a reminder that even logistics data has a supply chain.
essay.why: This is the geometry of impatience: a warehouse within a night's drive of nearly every American. The network follows interstates the way veins follow bone — I-70, I-80, the Inland Empire, the Lehigh Valley. Toggle Loss on top and see the same corridors twice: the roads that deliver everything also collect their toll.

layers.title: Every Fatal Crash of 2023
layers.caveat: 129 crashes (136 deaths) had no usable coordinates and are not shown

essay.what: Every located fatal traffic crash in the United States in 2023: 37,640 crashes, 40,889 deaths, one point each, from NHTSA's Fatality Analysis Reporting System. This is the most complete map of American grief published every year — and almost no one ever looks at it.
essay.how: The FARS national accident file, with 129 unlocatable crashes (136 deaths) excluded and disclosed. Each point is one crash; where the red brightens, deaths overlap. About 112 people died on the roads every single day of 2023.
essay.why: Loss is not scattered at random — it traces our infrastructure exactly. The red follows every highway, pools at intersections and city edges, thins where nobody drives. Zoom in anywhere and you are looking at ordinary trips: commutes, errands, the drive home. The shape of this layer is simply the shape of daily life, drawn in its worst outcomes.

layers.title: The Year Without Goodbyes
layers.statline: COVID-19 deaths in {n} counties, per 100,000 residents
layers.caveat: deaths as states reported them, by county of residence; small counties rest on a few deaths (counts shown); Kansas City and Joplin, Mo. are reported apart from their counties

essay.what: 1,122,747 deaths from COVID-19 in 3,137 counties, January 2020 to March 2023, shown as deaths per 100,000 residents. The bar steps through thirteen quarters so the waves can be watched moving: New Jersey, New York and southwest Georgia in the spring of 2020, Texas and the Deep South that summer, the Dakotas and the northern plains that winter. Some states reported deaths in batches long after they happened: when one whole state lights at once (Kansas in 2021 Q2, Nebraska in 2022 Q4), it may be paperwork arriving rather than a wave.
essay.how: The New York Times' county-level counts, compiled from state and local health departments, differenced into deaths per quarter and divided by each county's 2020 Census population. New York City's five boroughs are reported together, so each borough shows the city's combined rate. Licensed for non-commercial use with credit to The New York Times — this survey is non-commercial.
essay.why: No one is named here, and no one needs to be. The pale counties of the high plains are not spared places; they are places where a few deaths are a large share of everyone. Read with the Quiet Hours and the overdose layer, this is the survey's map of absence: chairs that stayed empty at tables the rest of the map never sees.

layers.title: Devil's Land, Angel's Land
layers.caveat: natural features and settlements only; word-boundary matching

essay.what: Every natural feature and settlement in America officially named for the beyond: 1,922 for devils, hell, and purgatory; 809 for angels, paradise, and Eden. Devils Canyon. Hells Half Acre. Angel Ridge. Paradise Valley.
essay.how: Word-boundary search across all 981,698 official names in the USGS Geographic Names Information System, restricted to natural features and populated places — no churches, no schools, nothing self-named. Red points are the dark names; bone-white points are the light ones.
essay.why: Surveyors named what they felt. The devils cluster in the hard land — the canyons, buttes, and badlands of the arid West, where the ground itself seemed hostile — while the angels settle in gentler valleys. Fear got the dramatic terrain; hope got the farmland. The final ratio is 2.4 devils for every angel, which may be the most honest theological statement America has ever made. Split by feature and the pattern sharpens: 89% of the Gaps and 84% of the Ridges belong to the devil, while 86% of the Towns took an angel's or a paradise's name. We fear the passes and bless the places we live.

layers.title: The Sky Is Watching Back
layers.caveat: self-reported testimony, geocoded to towns; corpus frozen mid-2014; reporting bias toward population and internet access

essay.what: 80,331 UFO sightings reported to the National UFO Reporting Center between 1906 and 2014, each with a mappable location — strange lights, discs, triangles, and orbs; every point a moment when somebody looked up and could not explain what they saw. The Phoenix Lights of March 1997 are in here, a tight knot of triangles over Arizona.
essay.how: The open community-geocoded NUFORC corpus (consolidated June 2014, checksum-verified). Reports are self-submitted and located to the nearest town. This layer maps testimony, not verified phenomena — which is exactly what makes it a soul measurement. Since v0.7 the plate carries a shape lens (light, triangle, circle, fireball, disk…), and the bar at the foot of the map steps through the decades the reports were filed. Reports are grouped by place to 0.01°, so one glow can hold many nights.
essay.why: Wonder has a geography, and it looks suspiciously like population plus darkness plus loneliness. The sightings trace where people live and where the sky is big enough to watch. The map says less about visitors than about who is looking up — and how badly they want an answer.

layers.title: The Last Dark
layers.statline: {n} places that promised to keep the night
layers.caveat: from Wikidata, which records only part of DarkSky International's register (darksky.org refuses scripts); one point per place, though reserves span whole regions

essay.what: The places that have promised to keep the night: parks, reserves, sanctuaries and whole towns certified for dark skies, from Natural Bridges in Utah (the first, in 2007) to Aoraki Mackenzie in New Zealand. Turn on the World's Furnaces and the data centers beside it: the dark places are what is left between the lights.
essay.how: Wikidata's records of International Dark Sky Parks, Reserves, Sanctuaries, Communities and Urban Night Sky Places, plus items it calls dark-sky preserves (CC0). DarkSky International's own register sits behind a bot check that the survey does not get around, so this is a partial mirror: the real count is higher, and the gaps are Wikidata's, not the sky's.
essay.why: Most of the light layers on this map are ones we did not choose — crashes, overdoses, furnaces. These points were chosen. A town that dims its streetlights so its children can see the Milky Way is a small, stubborn kind of wonder, and it belongs on a survey of the soul.

layers.title: The Quiet Epidemic
layers.caveat: rates, not raw counts; small counties may be modeled or suppressed

essay.what: 2024 drug overdose death rates for 3,014 US counties — the per-capita geography of the deadliest drug crisis in American history, tinted deeper violet as the rate climbs. The highest rate in the nation is Knott County, Kentucky: 139.1 deaths per 100,000.
essay.how: CDC's Mapping Injury, Overdose, and Violence county dataset (calendar year 2024, crude rates per 100k; smaller counties use CDC's own Bayesian smoothing, disclosed). 129 counties with suppressed counts stay dark and are counted honestly rather than smoothed over.
essay.why: The epidemic is not random — half of the hundred worst county rates sit in five Appalachian states. But this survey's first draft claimed despair pools farthest from the money, and the data overruled it: rates run higher near Fortune 500 headquarters than far from them, and Baltimore holds one of the worst rates in the nation. The crisis is rural and metropolitan at once — see The Folklore Fails in the Findings. One hopeful note lives in this vintage: 2024 saw the largest one-year national decline on record.

layers.title: What We Buried
layers.caveat: National Priorities List only — thousands of lesser Superfund-program sites are not shown

essay.what: All 1,840 sites of the EPA's National Priorities List — the most contaminated ground in America: mines, smelters, chemical plants, landfills, military ranges. Love Canal is here. So is the Butte pit complex, and Hanford four times over.
essay.how: EPA's own NPL inventory with coordinates (the dataset behind its Superfund 'Where You Live' map), statuses normalized to proposed (37), final (1,343), and deleted (460) — where deleted means cleaned up enough to leave the list, not erased from the ground. The bar replays the list itself: a site appears the year EPA listed it and leaves the map the year it was deleted, so 1983's 406 standing sites become 1,343 today. Forty-two sites have no listing date in the inventory (37 still proposed, 5 deleted) and never appear on the bar.
essay.why: Industry leaves a residue that outlives the industry: acid in the aquifer, lead in the yard soil, a fence around a field. The acid-yellow points cluster where America made things and walked away. Stack them on the Thrones of Capital and you are looking at the before and after of the same story.

layers.title: The Quiet Hours
layers.protocol: If you or someone you know is struggling, call or text 988 — the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. This layer shows rates for places, never points for people.
layers.caveat: pooled multi-year rates; suppressed counties stay dark by law and by principle; groups, never individuals

essay.what: Suicide mortality rates for 2,448 US counties, pooled over five years (2018–2022) so that small places can be shown honestly. Another 704 counties stay dark — their counts fall under the federal confidentiality floor, and the survey keeps them dark rather than estimate. Every value is a rate for a place. Nothing on this map is a person.
essay.how: NCHS vital-statistics mortality via County Health Rankings' open analytic release, age-adjusted, with every suppression rule honored and independently re-verified (no published county sits under ten pooled deaths). A note on gates: CDC's own WONDER API refuses sub-national mortality queries by deliberate policy — the browser-only rule is real, and it shaped this acquisition. State youth rates remain a disclosed gap on this plate until the WISQARS path is completed. Safe-messaging practice governs all copy: no methods, no simple causes.
essay.why: The quietest layer in the survey, and the one that most needed the heat-not-points rule. The geography is real — western Alaska, the northern plains, the Mountain West carry rates the coasts do not — and it coincides with distance: from care, from neighbors, from the nearest bright cluster on every other layer of this map. Where, not why, was never more important.

layers.title: The Great Sorting
layers.caveat: IRS tax-filer data — the poorest and richest households are undercounted; households, not people, unless noted

essay.what: County-to-county migration drawn from IRS tax returns: the survey's first flow map. Teal counties gained households on net; ember counties lost them. The arcs are the largest corridors — each one thousands of actual moves.
essay.how: IRS Statistics of Income migration files, latest filing-year pair. Same-county and summary rows excluded per the file layout; corridors kept above a disclosed household threshold so the map stays legible. Tax-filer data undercounts the poorest and the richest; that caveat rides on every number. COUNT switches between households (tax returns) and people (exemptions claimed): the same IRS rows in a different unit, and only the second counts children and other dependents.
essay.why: This is the country rearranging itself in real time — out of the old cores, into the Sun Belt, following rent and work and weather. Toggle the thrones or the fulfillment network underneath and watch what the movers are moving toward. Every arc is a bet that somewhere else is better.

layers.title: The Price of Staying
layers.caveat: modelled estimates (Eviction Lab, 2022); a threat is a court filing against a household, not always a removal; ends in 2018

time.label: Threatened in the year, per 100 renting households

essay.what: How often a renting household is taken to court to be put out: households threatened with eviction each year per 100 renting households, in 3,142 counties from 2000 to 2018. The median county sits near 2.6; the worst counties are ten times higher. About 3.7 million eviction cases were filed in an average year.
essay.how: The Princeton Eviction Lab's model estimates (Gromis, Fellows, Hendrickson, Edmonds, Leung, Porton & Desmond, 2022), which combine court records with a statistical model to fill counties whose courts do not report, published under ODC-BY 1.0. The map pools 2014–2018; the bar steps through each year. Maryland fills the top of the list: its rent courts let a landlord file again every month rent is late, so the same household is threatened many times over.
essay.why: Eviction is the sorting seen from below. The Great Sorting shows who leaves by choice; this shows who is pushed — densest in Maryland, the Virginia and Carolina cities, the Atlanta suburbs and the Deep South. Richmond, Petersburg and Clayton County, Georgia sit near the top; the Dakotas and Wyoming barely register.

layers.title: The Sky Roads
layers.statline: {n} air corridors flown by two or more airlines
layers.caveat: a historic snapshot (OpenFlights route data, about 2014, no longer maintained); airline count, not passengers; single-airline routes not drawn

essay.what: 8,362 air corridors, each flown by at least two airlines, drawn as great circles between their airports. The brightest arcs carry the most airlines: the trunk routes of Europe, the North Atlantic, the Gulf, East Asia. Atlanta, Chicago, Beijing, London and Paris are the knots with the most routes.
essay.how: OpenFlights' route database — 67,663 airline routes between 3,321 airports, from Airline Route Mapper — folded into airport pairs and weighted by how many airlines fly each one. Licensed ODbL with contents under the DbCL, so this derived layer is offered under the same terms. The route file has not been maintained for years: read it as a snapshot of about 2014. The 10,496 pairs flown by a single airline are left off to keep the arcs legible.
essay.why: The logistics bloodstream has an upper atmosphere. Lay it over the Last Speakers and the two maps of connection barely touch: the arcs crowd where a few large languages are spoken, and thin out over New Guinea, the Amazon and the Sahel, where languages are most numerous.

layers.title: The Uprooted
layers.statline: {n} corridors of the displaced, end of 2024
layers.caveat: people living outside their country at end-2024 (stocks, not movements in the year); country centroids, not camps; Palestine refugees under UNRWA are outside UNHCR's count; corridors under 500 people not drawn

essay.what: 44.8 million people living outside the country they fled at the end of 2024 — refugees, asylum-seekers and others UNHCR counts as needing international protection — drawn as arcs from where they came from to where they are now. The 1,155 corridors of 500 people or more carry more than 99% of them. The brightest ends are where the arcs land: next door, far more often than across an ocean.
essay.how: UNHCR's Refugee Population Statistics Database, read through its public API (CC BY 4.0 under UNHCR's Terms of Use for Datasets). Each origin–asylum pair is summed across refugees, asylum-seekers and other people in need of international protection — the category that holds most displaced Venezuelans. Arcs run between country centroids on the map's own shapes; 254,406 people of unknown origin and 41,083 stateless people have no starting point and are not drawn.
essay.why: Venezuela (7.6 million), Afghanistan, Syria and Ukraine (5 to 6 million each) empty outward; Iran, Türkiye, Germany, Colombia and Uganda take the most in, and the United States leads the hosts mainly through pending asylum claims. Most of the uprooted live one border away. Lay the World at War beneath it: the arcs start where the reds are.

layers.title: The Company We Keep
layers.caveat: derived from Facebook friendships, adults 25–44; measures cross-class friendship, not warmth

essay.what: Economic connectedness by county, from the Social Capital Atlas: the share of above-median-income friends in below-median-income people's networks — the strongest known community-level predictor of a poor child's chance of rising.
essay.how: Chetty et al. (2022), built from anonymized Facebook friendship graphs for adults 25–44, published openly with differential-privacy noise. The measure is calibrated so 1.0 means class-blind friendship; the real range runs 0.29 to 1.36. Rose wash deepens where cross-class friendship is thick. It measures who knows whom — not kindness, not warmth, and only among people on the platform.
essay.why: The loneliness layer, inverted: this is where the bridges are. Lay it over Despair and the argument starts by itself — the places where classes actually befriend each other are rarely the places the epidemics chose. Where the wash runs thin, the ladder is missing a rung.

layers.title: The Arsenal
layers.pendingNote: Source verified open (ATF monthly FFL lists) but served behind a browser-only gate that outlasted this survey window. The ZIP gazetteer is staged; the slot is reserved for the retry.
layers.caveat: retail license types 01 and 02 only; ZIP-centroid locations aggregated to cells

essay.what: Every federally licensed retail firearms dealer and pawnbroker in America, aggregated to cells — the storefront geography of the Second Amendment.
essay.how: ATF's monthly Federal Firearms Licensee listing, types 01 and 02, geocoded by premise ZIP and binned so the page stays light. Counts are of licenses, not guns; a cell's glow is commerce, not crime.
essay.why: The arsenal is not where the fear is loudest on television — it follows highways and county seats, a hardware-store geography. Pair it with the Altar and the two devotions of the interior sit side by side; pair it with Loss and hold your judgment: the survey shows where, never why.

layers.title: When the State Kills
layers.statline: people shot dead by police, 2015–2024, per county
layers.protocol: Rates for places, never points for people. Every number here is someone; none of them is named on this map.
layers.caveat: fatal shootings by on-duty police only (The Washington Post's scope); small counties rest on one or two deaths (counts shown); 1.6% of records could not be placed in a county

essay.what: 10,268 people shot and killed by on-duty police officers in the United States from 2015 to 2024, placed in the county where it happened and divided by its population: about a thousand a year, every year, and rising after 2022. The map shows rates per 100,000 residents over the decade; the bar shows each year per million.
essay.how: The Washington Post's Fatal Force database, which has logged every such killing since 2015 from news reports, public records and social media, licensed CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0 (this derived layer carries the same licence). Names, ages, race and exact locations are dropped before anything else happens; only counts per county and year are kept. Records are placed by their coordinates, else their county, else their city's centre; 162 could not be placed. Deaths by restraint, Tasers or vehicles are outside the Post's count.
essay.why: The highest rates are not where the crime headlines are. New Mexico (10.1 per 100,000 over the decade) and Alaska (9.1) lead the states, then Oklahoma and Colorado; Rhode Island, Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York sit near one — a tenfold gap inside one country, under one constitution. The map says where; the why is argued elsewhere, and the survey does not pretend to settle it.

layers.title: The World at War
layers.protocol: Rates for countries, never points for people. No victim, perpetrator or place is named.
layers.caveat: UCDP best estimates of deaths in organized violence (state, non-state and one-sided); today's borders and today's populations; periods of five years

essay.what: 4.26 million people killed in organized violence since 1989 — wars between states and rebels, wars between armed groups, and massacres of civilians — in 119 countries, shown per 100,000 of today's population. The bar steps through five-year periods: Rwanda and Bosnia in the early 1990s, Congo at the decade's end, Ethiopia at the turn of the century, Syria through the 2010s, Ethiopia's Tigray war and Ukraine in the 2020s, Ukraine and Sudan in 2025.
essay.how: The Uppsala Conflict Data Program's Georeferenced Event Dataset 26.1 (CC BY 4.0): every event's best estimate of deaths, summed by country and period. Each GED country is matched to the map's own country shapes by its events' coordinates; populations are Wikidata's latest figures, one denominator for the whole span (so 1990s rates use today's population). Actors, places and sources are dropped.
essay.why: The survey's other layers are mostly about how people live; this one is about how many were not allowed to. Rwanda's 1994 rate — more than five thousand per hundred thousand in five years — is the darkest cell anywhere on the map. Read it with the Last Speakers: several of the deepest reds sit on the same ground as the languages closest to silence.

layers.title: The Altar
layers.caveat: congregation-reported adherence, 2020 census; traditions self-define membership; ~1% of counties exceed 1,000 per 1k where regional congregations draw worshippers across county lines

essay.what: Religious adherents per thousand residents in every county, from the 2020 U.S. Religion Census — the candle-gold wash of organized belief, with each county's largest tradition on the tooltip.
essay.how: Congregation-by-congregation counts assembled by the religion census, published at county level. Adherence is what congregations report; traditions define membership differently, and the unaffiliated are the negative space. SHADE BY switches the map from adherents per 1,000 to each county's largest tradition family, drawn in nine colours from the same Religion Census group table.
essay.why: The altar's geography is older than any other layer here — Utah's wash, the Baptist South, the Lutheran upper plains, the Catholic border counties are all still exactly where the nineteenth century left them. Belief, it turns out, is the slowest-moving thing the survey has ever mapped.

layers.title: The Ledger of Betrayals
layers.caveat: convicted or pled only; court-established amounts; every entry carries citations in the staging data

essay.what: The great municipal frauds of America, curated one conviction at a time: who stole, from which town, how much, for how long, and what it cost them. Dixon, Illinois anchors the ledger — $53.7 million over 22 years, a comptroller, and a stable of champion horses.
essay.how: Built by hand from Justice Department releases, court records, and major-outlet reporting; no dataset of this existed, so the survey made one. Only the convicted are named. Every entry ships with its citations. Amounts are court-established.
essay.why: Every coin-gold point is a place that trusted somebody with the books. Small towns dominate the ledger not because small towns are corrupt but because one person there IS the controls — the auditor, the treasurer, and the alarm, all in the same chair. This layer is what it costs when nobody is watching the watcher.

layers.title: Notice of Mass Layoff
layers.caveat: sources gated; nothing shown rather than something invented
layers.pendingNote: Standardized WARN notice data is gated (commercial paywall / authenticated academic access). The registry slot is reserved; the survey continues.

essay.what: Mass-layoff (WARN) notices by state — where the jobs vanish, in aggregate. Pending: the standardized multi-state datasets are currently paywalled or access-gated.
essay.how: This layer will aggregate trailing-12-month WARN notices per 100k residents once an open standardized source is secured. No questionable numbers were shipped in the meantime.
essay.why: A survey that fakes a layer betrays all the others. This slot stays visibly empty as a promise: the map is built to keep growing, honestly.
